newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Time running out for Brazil's ailing reforms.
newsitem.headline: Time running out for Brazil's ailing reforms.

text.p: The Brazilian government appears to be running out of time to get key structural reforms through Congress and may have to resort to special measures to get them approved in 1999, lawmakers and analysts said.

Nearly two years after they were sent to parliament, reforms of the civil service and the pensions system, both of which are considered essential to Brazil's long-term economic stability, are still a long way off being approved.
Officials say the reforms must be passed by September when the Brazilian political scene will be absorbed by next year's presidential, congressional and state governorship elections.

Newspapers reported Friday that government-allied whips were seeking to water down the already diluted civil service reform bill, especially its most controversial clause to end lifetime job guarantees for civil servants.

The measure was seen as a last-gasp attempt to get the bill approved next week in the Chamber of Deputies and into the Senate where opposition should be less intense. The government may also cancel the month-long recess in July to boost its chances of getting the reform approved.
A pension reform bill is considered even less likely to make it through Congress before the elections.

It is currently before a Senate committee and requires two votes on the floor of the upper house before going back to the rowdy Chamber of Deputies, which struck down its most important points last year, for approval of changes to the bill.

"Our outlook is very negative," said Jose Carlos Faria, an economic analyst with ING Barings in Sao Paulo. "The government put all its emphasis on the reforms and now it will have to find another way of reducing the (public sector) deficit."
Government lawmakers, who insisted for months they would win their reform battle, have recently adopted a more sombre tone.
"We cannot deny the reforms have been undermined," said Aecio Neves, the lower house leader of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB).

On Wednesday, shortly after whips abandoned yet another session aimed at voting on civil service reform, Neves announced the government was preparing a bill that would make it easier to approve constitutional reform during a special, one-year period.
During a "revisory" session of Congress, the constitution can be changed with only a straight majority of votes in the Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate.
Normally, constitutional amendments need two three-fifths majorities in each house, a challenge that has frustrated the government's hopes for civil service and pension reform.

To call the revisory session, which would run throughout 1999, the first year of the next Congress, the government would have to approve a constitutional amendment in the current session of parliament with the normal three-fifths majorities.

Neves also said the government intended to hold a referendum on the issue which would take place on election day in October next year. "The referendum could do away with a lot of resistance in the next Congress to deep reform," he said.

Not everyone is so enthusiastic about a revisory Congress. Legal experts have suggested it may be unconstitutional. Cardoso himself sounded a cautionary note Friday, warning that the move could set a precedent for frequent constitutional revisions.
"If we allow the constitution to be changed, we could create a lot of instability," the president told national Jovem Pan radio in an interview.

"It would be easier to change internal, congressional rules," Cardoso added, suggesting a review of the way opposition parties can bog down reforms, and often defeat their most important points without a majority, via amendments.
